bills.title: To amend the FISA Amendments Act of 2008 to extend the authorities of title VII of the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act of 1978 through April 30, 2026, and for other purposes.
bills.official_title: To amend the FISA Amendments Act of 2008 to extend the authorities of title VII of the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act of 1978 through April 30, 2026, and for other purposes.
bills.summary: Amends the FISA Amendments Act of 2008 to replace the rolling two-year repeal date for Title VII of the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act of 1978 (50 U.S.C. 1881 et seq.) with a fixed deadline of April 30, 2026. The bill was introduced on April 16, signed into law as Public Law 119-84 on April 18, 2026, and contains no new reform provisions or oversight requirements.
bills.brief: Extends Title VII of FISA warrantless surveillance authorities through April 30, 2026 with no reforms attached.

top_lines.headline: Surveillance Reauthorization
subs: Replaces the prior rolling repeal date for Title VII of FISA (50 U.S.C. 1881 et seq.) with a fixed April 30, 2026 deadline
No new oversight requirements, reform provisions, or privacy protections included in the extension

top_lines.headline: Rapid Enactment
subs: Introduced April 16, 2026 and signed into law as Public Law 119-84 on April 18, 2026 — two days from introduction to enactment

bills.likelihoodReason: Signed into law by the President on April 18, 2026 as Public Law 119-84.

sections.label: Section 1 — Extension of Title VII Repeal Date

items.main: Amends Section 403(b)(1) of the FISA Amendments Act of 2008 (Public Law 110-261) to set the repeal date of Title VII of the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act of 1978 at April 30, 2026.
items.detail: Prior law set the repeal date at two years after enactment of the Reforming Intelligence and Securing America Act. This amendment replaces that rolling deadline with a fixed April 30, 2026 date. The amendment takes effect on the earlier of the date of enactment of this Act or April 19, 2026.

items.main: Amends Section 404(b) of the FISA Amendments Act of 2008 to update citation references in the transition procedures to cite 50 U.S.C. 1881 et seq. directly.
items.detail: Two subsections of Section 404(b) are amended by removing references to the FISA Amendments Reauthorization Act of 2017 and the Reforming Intelligence and Securing America Act, replacing them with a direct citation to 50 U.S.C. 1881 et seq. The heading of one amended paragraph is updated from a reference to the prior act enactment date to the term repeal date.

underreported.summary: Section 1(b) amends the transition procedures in Section 404(b) of the FISA Amendments Act of 2008 by removing references to specific prior reauthorization acts and substituting a direct citation to 50 U.S.C. 1881 et seq. The heading of one amended paragraph is changed from a date-based label to the term repeal date.
underreported.why_unreported: Section 1(b) is labeled as extending transition procedures, but its operative text removes amendment-chain citation references rather than changing any substantive rule. The update governs which statutory reference applies to the transition procedures when Title VII expires or is further amended.

criticisms.why: Opposed reauthorization without reform, stating that a straight extension of FISA law is absolutely unacceptable and that warrantless searches tripled in the first year of the Trump administration.

gaps: The bill extends Title VII surveillance authorities through April 30, 2026 but sets no reporting requirement on how those authorities are used during the extension period.
The bill replaces the prior rolling deadline with a fixed date but does not establish any conditions or review process governing further reauthorization after April 30, 2026.

The bill amends the repeal date and transition procedure citations but does not address the status of any outstanding directives if the April 30, 2026 deadline passes without further action by Congress.

featured_quotes.name: Sen. Ron Wyden
featured_quotes.text: Any Senator who votes to reauthorize this law without real reform will be directly responsible when the Trump team abuses their spying powers.

featured_quotes.name: Sen. Ron Wyden
featured_quotes.text: The number of so-called 'sensitive' warrantless searches more than tripled during the first year of the Trump administration.

modified: Section 403(b)(1) of the FISA Amendments Act of 2008 (Public Law 110-261) — Title VII repeal date changed from two years after enactment of the Reforming Intelligence and Securing America Act to April 30, 2026

Section 404(b) of the FISA Amendments Act of 2008 — transition procedure citation references updated to 50 U.S.C. 1881 et seq., removing references to the FISA Amendments Reauthorization Act of 2017 and the Reforming Intelligence and Securing America Act

bills.title: Directing the President, pursuant to section 5(c) of the War Powers Resolution, to remove United States Armed Forces from hostilities with Iran.
bills.official_title: Directing the President, pursuant to section 5(c) of the War Powers Resolution, to remove United States Armed Forces from hostilities with Iran.
bills.summary: Directs the President to remove United States Armed Forces from hostilities against the Islamic Republic of Iran under section 5(c) of the War Powers Resolution (50 U.S.C. 1544(c)). Forces required to defend the United States, an ally, or a partner from imminent attack may remain, provided the President fully complies with the 60-day withdrawal requirement in section 5(b) of the War Powers Resolution. Continued operations against Iran require either a declaration of war or a specific congressional authorization for use of military force.
bills.brief: Invokes the War Powers Resolution to direct the President to end U.S. military operations against Iran without a declaration of war or specific congressional authorization.

top_lines.headline: War Powers Directive
subs: Directs the President to remove U.S. Armed Forces from hostilities against the Islamic Republic of Iran under section 5(c) of the War Powers Resolution (50 U.S.C. 1544(c))
Carve-out for forces defending the United States, an ally, or a partner from imminent attack, conditioned on the President complying with section 5(b) of the War Powers Resolution (50 U.S.C. 1544(b))

top_lines.headline: Authorization Threshold
subs: Military operations against Iran may continue only if authorized by a declaration of war or a specific congressional authorization for use of military force against Iran
90 cosponsors in the House; passed April 16, 2026

bills.likelihoodReason: The resolution passed the House with 90 cosponsors indicating bipartisan support. However, the Senate is controlled by Republicans who are unlikely to advance a concurrent resolution challenging a Republican president's conduct of military operations. Concurrent war powers resolutions rarely clear the Senate when the president's party holds the majority.

sections.label: Resolving Clause — Withdrawal from Iran Hostilities

items.main: Congress directs the President to remove U.S. Armed Forces from hostilities against the Islamic Republic of Iran under section 5(c) of the War Powers Resolution (50 U.S.C. 1544(c)).
items.detail: The directive exempts forces necessary to defend the United States, an ally, or a partner from imminent attack, provided the President fully complies with section 5(b) of the War Powers Resolution (50 U.S.C. 1544(b)). Section 5(b) generally requires removal of forces within 60 days of their introduction into hostilities unless Congress authorizes continued engagement. Continued operations require explicit authorization through a declaration of war or a specific authorization for use of military force against Iran.

comments.text: Rep. Gregory Meeks (D-NY): One person does not have the power to take this Nation to war alone.
Rep. Keith Self (R-TX): We have neutered Iran, which has been at war with us for 47 years.

underreported.summary: The resolution permits forces to remain if needed to defend the United States, an ally, or a partner from imminent attack, conditioned on the President complying with section 5(b) of the War Powers Resolution.
underreported.why_unreported: The term imminent attack is not defined in the resolution. The resolution does not specify who determines when a threat qualifies as imminent or what evidence is required, leaving that threshold determination entirely to the executive branch.

criticisms.why: Opposed the withdrawal directive on grounds that U.S. military operations had achieved a strategic objective against Iran.

gaps: The resolution directs withdrawal from hostilities against the Islamic Republic of Iran but does not define what operations constitute hostilities, a term whose scope the resolution does not address.
The resolution invokes section 5(c) of the War Powers Resolution but does not specify a timeline by which the President must comply after the directive is transmitted.

The resolution's imminent attack exception covers forces defending an ally or partner of the United States but does not specify which allies or partners qualify or how eligibility for the exception is determined.

featured_quotes.text: The war has cost taxpayers $50 billion already, and the Pentagon will request $200 billion more.

featured_quotes.text: One person does not have the power to take this Nation to war alone.

featured_quotes.text: We have neutered Iran, which has been at war with us for 47 years.

bills.title: Main Street Capital Access Act
bills.likelihoodReason: Rep. Hill (R-AR), Chair of the House Financial Services Committee, sponsored this bill with 33 Republican cosponsors and zero Democratic support — a strictly partisan track. House passage is plausible given the Republican majority, but Senate passage requires 60 votes to overcome a filibuster, and the complete absence of Democratic cosponsors signals no crossover appeal. The CBLR capital floor reduction and the one-way GDP ratchet will draw organized opposition from consumer protection and banking reform groups, making Senate passage unlikely without significant amendment.

sections.label: Title I — New Bank Formation and Local Community Access

items.main: New rural depository institutions (under $10B total assets) receive a 3-year capital phase-in with CBLR capped at the lesser of the standard rate or 7.5%
items.detail: Rural defined as county outside metropolitan or micropolitan statistical area per OMB Urban Influence Codes, or census block not in urban area per latest Census. Business plan deviations must be approved, conditionally approved, or denied within 30 days — failure to act is deemed approval. Federal banking agencies must jointly study de novo bank formation barriers and report to Congress within 1 year of enactment.

items.main: CDFI Bond Guarantee Program annual cap set at $1B with $25M minimum per transaction; guarantee fees range 10–15 basis points; program extended through December 31, 2028
items.detail: Section 106 amends Section 114A, Community Development Banking and Financial Institutions Act of 1994 (12 U.S.C. 4713a). Secretary of Treasury must issue a report to Congress on program effectiveness not later than 3 years after enactment. The Sense of Congress affirms the program furthers the CDFI Fund mission to increase economic opportunity for underserved populations and distressed communities.

items.main: National bank investment threshold in bank premises raised from 15% to 20% in both Section 5136 of the Revised Statutes (12 U.S.C. 24) and Section 9 of the Federal Reserve Act (12 U.S.C. 338a)
items.detail: Section 104 strikes "15" and inserts "20" in the fifth sentence of each provision, expanding how much of a national bank's capital can be committed to physical assets. Section 105 adds a requirement that the CDFI Fund Secretary annually testify before Congressional financial committees at the discretion of committee chairs.

items.main: Community Bank Leverage Ratio eligibility threshold raised from $10B to $15B; qualifying capital ratio range changed from 8–10% to 6–9%
items.detail: Section 203 amends Section 201, Economic Growth, Regulatory Relief, and Consumer Protection Act (12 U.S.C. 5371 note). Agencies must propose rule changes within 180 days and finalize within 1 year. Board of Governors, OCC, and FDIC must review the CBLR and report to Congress within 150 days covering opt-in incentives, burden relief, and reporting simplification.

items.main: 47 thresholds across 14 federal statutes adjusted upward for historical GDP growth; all thresholds recalibrated every 5 years beginning April 1, 2031
items.detail: Representative adjustments under Section 205: CRA small bank threshold $250M → $800M; Federal Home Loan Bank membership $1B → $3B; FDIC independent audit threshold $150M → $800M; Depository Institution Management Interlocks Act threshold $100M → $600M; Home Mortgage Disclosure Act small institution threshold $30M → $160M. New Sections 177 and 178 of the Financial Stability Act of 2010 establish the GDP-indexed adjustment mechanism with rounding rules and Federal Register publication by April 5 of each adjustment year.

items.main: Small Bank Holding Company consolidated asset threshold raised to $6B; Board of Governors must revise Appendix C to Part 225, Title 12, Code of Federal Regulations within 180 days
items.detail: Appendix C is commonly known as the Small Bank Holding Company and Savings and Loan Holding Company Policy Statement. The higher threshold reduces holding company-level capital and debt issuance requirements for mid-size regional banks previously above the old threshold.

items.main: High-rated federal credit union board meetings reduced from monthly to a minimum of 6 times per year, with at least one meeting each fiscal quarter
items.detail: Section 206 amends Section 113 of the Federal Credit Union Act (12 U.S.C. 1761b). Applies only to credit unions with CAMELS composite rating of 1 or 2 AND capability of management rating of 1 or 2. De novo federal credit unions retain the monthly requirement for their first 5 years. Credit unions with composite or management rating of 3, 4, or 5 retain the monthly requirement.

sections.label: Title III — Fair and Transparent Bank Supervision

items.main: Federal Financial Institutions Examination Council required to reform CAMELS rating system to use articulable, clear, and reviewable criteria; management component must be either eliminated or limited to objective governance measures
items.detail: Section 301 adds new Section 1012 to the Federal Financial Institutions Examination Council Act of 1978 (12 U.S.C. 3301 et seq.). Revised criteria must ensure composite ratings reflect material financial condition and solvency, incorporate compliance with anti-money laundering requirements (Section 21, Federal Deposit Insurance Act; Subchapter II, Chapter 53, Title 31 U.S.C.), and use transparent methodology limited to objective CAMELS component criteria. Congress finds CAMELS currently relies on examiner judgment leading to subjective and inconsistent ratings.

underreported.section: Section 104 — National Bank Investment in Bank Premises
underreported.summary: Raises the national bank investment limit in physical bank premises from 15% to 20%, expanding how much of a national bank's capital can be held in illiquid property assets.
underreported.why_unreported: Section 104 is labeled "Community Investment and Prosperity" and appears among CDFI and rural banking provisions. The operative text is a two-word substitution ("15" → "20") with no accompanying analysis or impact statement in the section.

underreported.section: Section 203 — CBLR Qualifying Capital Ratio Lower Bound
underreported.summary: The qualifying Community Bank Leverage Ratio lower bound drops from 8% to 6%, expanding the range of institutions that qualify for simplified supervision to include banks with capital ratios as low as 6%.
underreported.why_unreported: Section 203 is titled "Community Bank Leverage Improvement and Flexibility" and the primary stated goal is raising the $10B eligibility threshold. The reduction in the qualifying capital ratio floor appears in the same subsection but is not referenced in the section heading or stated findings.

underreported.summary: The GDP adjustment mechanism in Sections 177–178 of the Financial Stability Act requires thresholds to increase when GDP grows but contains no provision for reducing thresholds if GDP contracts or reverses.
underreported.why_unreported: Sections 177(a) and 178(b) specify adjustments by the ratio "if greater than 1" — meaning adjustments only apply when GDP has grown. The condition is stated in the operative text but not in the section titles or congressional findings accompanying Section 204.

gaps: Title I is captioned "Local Community Access" but the rural area definition references OMB Urban Influence Codes and Census urban areas — neither of which covers U.S. territories, which are not addressed in the bill's rural bank formation provisions.

Section 203 requires agencies to review the CBLR and report recommendations, but specifies no consumer impact assessment as part of that review despite Section 201(a)(3)(A) requiring agencies to consider the aggregate effect of regulatory actions on ability to serve customers.

Section 205 raises the CRA small bank threshold from $250,000,000 to $800,000,000, but contains no corresponding update to the CRA examination frequency or reporting methodology for banks that now fall below the threshold.

Section 202 raises the Small Bank Holding Company consolidated asset threshold to $6,000,000,000 but does not specify whether existing holding companies that newly qualify must re-file or are automatically reclassified.

Full text of Titles IV–VIII (regulatory accountability, discount window, merger clarity, resolution transparency, bank-fintech partnerships) was not available for complete analysis — provisions in those titles may contain material changes not reflected here.
bills.brief: Raises 47 regulatory thresholds across 14 federal statutes and indexes all of them to GDP — adjusting every 5 years starting April 1, 2031 — to reduce compliance costs on community banks and credit unions.

bills.summary: The Main Street Capital Access Act is a comprehensive banking deregulation bill that raises dozens of regulatory thresholds across 14 federal statutes to match GDP growth, eases capital requirements for new community banks, reforms the CDFI Bond Guarantee Program, and requires federal examiners to tailor supervision to each institution's actual risk profile.

bills.title: Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2026

bills.summary: This act reduces taxes, increases spending for various federal programs, and addresses agencies throughout the federal government as a reconciliation bill.
bills.brief: The bill provides tax cuts, modifies federal spending on agriculture, energy, and conservation, and adjusts immigration fees.
top_lines: Increases LIP payment rate to 100% for losses due to predation (from 75%).
Reduces cap on earnings transferred from Federal Reserve Board to CFPB from 12% to 6.5%.
Modifies Gulf of Mexico Energy Security Act of 2006 to raise cap on distribution of OCS revenues to oil and gas producing Gulf states from $500 million to $650 million per year for FY2025-FY34.
bills.likelihoodReason: The bill has already become Public Law No: 119-21, indicating it was enacted. The sponsor is a Republican from Texas with zero cosponsors, but the reconciliation process and the fact that it became law suggest broad support or procedural necessity.

sections.label: Title I — COMMITTEE ON AGRICULTURE, NUTRITION, AND FORESTRY

items.main: Increases the payment rate under the Livestock Indemnity Program (LIP) to 100% for losses due to predation.
items.detail: Modifies the LIP payment rate for predation losses from 75% to 100%. The text cuts off mid-sentence regarding 'attacks by animals reintroduced'.

items.main: Reduces the cap on the percentage of combined earnings transferred from the Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve to the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (CFPB).
items.detail: Changes the cap on earnings transferred from the Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve to the CFPB from 12% to 6.5%. The text cuts off before completing the provision.

items.main: Reduces restrictions on onshore development of oil and gas on federal lands by decreasing minimum royalty rates, reinstating noncompetitive leasing, directing Interior to resume quarterly lease sales in specified states, and approving applications allowing commingling of production from two or more sources before royalty payment measurement.
items.detail: Modifies existing restrictions on federal land oil and gas development. No new programs created; existing leasing practices modified (noncompetitive leasing reinstated).

sections.label: Title II — TAX POLICY AND REVENUE

items.main: Increases the percentage rate to 50% (from 25%) at which the alternative minimum tax exemption amount is phased out for individuals whose taxable income exceeds such threshold amount.
items.detail: The alternative minimum taxable income threshold amounts are $626,350 or $1,252,700 for joint filers for 2025, as adjusted annually for inflation beginning in 2026. Applies to individuals filing joint returns or married individuals filing separately.

items.main: Makes permanent the limit on the itemized tax deduction for home mortgage interest enacted in 2017 by the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act.
items.detail: Allows certain mortgage insurance premiums to be included in the itemized tax deduction for home mortgage interest. The limit is $750,000; $375,000 for married individuals filing separately.

items.main: Makes permanent and increases the tax deduction for charitable contributions made by individuals who do not itemize their federal income tax deductions.
items.detail: Increases the deduction amount to $1,000 for single filers (from $300) and $2,000 for joint filers (from $600 for joint filers). Makes it permanent.

items.main: Establishes a fee of at least $100 for applications for asylum.
items.detail: Applies to applicants for asylum. Provides exceptions on a case-by-case basis for the fee established in Sec. 100004 (e.g., life-threatening medical emergency).

items.main: Establishes a fee of at least $550 for asylees, parolees, or individuals granted temporary protected status who are applying for initial employment authorization.
items.detail: Applies to asylees, parolees, or individuals granted temporary protected status applying for initial employment authorization. Provides exceptions on a case-by-case basis for the fee established in Sec. 100004 (e.g., life-threatening medical emergency).

items.main: Eliminates the exemption from certain duties, fees, and processes for imports of up to $800 (commonly referred to as the de minimis exemption), effective July 1, 2027.
items.detail: Establishes a civil penalty for using such exemption in a manner that violates U.S. customs laws. Penalty: up to $5,000 for the first violation and up to $10,000 for subsequent violations.

bills.official_title: An act to provide for reconciliation pursuant to title II of H. Con. Res. 14.

bills.summary: The HEATS Act waives federal drilling permit requirements for geothermal exploration and production on non-federal lands if the U.S. owns less than 50% of the subsurface estate and a state permit is submitted.
bills.brief: This bill exempts certain geothermal activities from federal permitting, environmental review, and historic preservation requirements.
top_lines: Waives Federal drilling permit requirement for qualifying geothermal activities on non-Federal surface estate
Exempts qualifying activities from NEPA section 102(2)(C) and Endangered Species Act section 7
U.S. ownership interest must be less than 50 percent of the subsurface geothermal estate
bills.likelihoodReason: The bill has only 2 cosponsors in the House, which is a very low number for passage. The sponsor is a Republican from California (R-CA), and the latest action shows a motion to reconsider was laid on the table without objection, indicating limited debate or support. The provision waives federal permitting requirements, which may attract opposition from environmental groups or representatives concerned about regulatory oversight.

sections.label: Title I — Harnessing Energy At Thermal Sources Act

items.main: Waives the requirement for a Federal drilling permit for geothermal exploration and production activities conducted on a non-Federal surface estate, provided that (1) the United States holds an ownership interest of less than 50 percent of the subsurface geothermal estate to be accessed by the proposed action; and (2) the operator submits to the Secretary a State permit to conduct geothermal exploration and production activities on the non-Federal surface estate.
items.detail: The bill amends the Geothermal Steam Act of 1970 by adding Section 30. It exempts such activity from NEPA section 102(2)(C) and Endangered Species Act section 7, subject to conditions. The Secretary may conduct onsite reviews and inspections for accountability, measurement, reporting, and royalty payment.

underreported.section: Section 30 of the Geothermal Steam Act of 1970
underreported.summary: The provision states that royalties due to the United States under this Act from production of electricity using geothermal resources (other than direct use) or byproducts are not affected.
underreported.why_unreported: Royalty obligations remain intact despite the waiver of drilling permits, which may be overlooked in summaries focusing solely on permitting relief.

gaps: The bill does not address potential impacts on tribal lands or resources managed in trust for Indian Tribes beyond simply excluding them from the waiver.
The bill does not specify how state permits are evaluated to ensure they meet environmental standards comparable to federal requirements.

added: New Section 30 in the Geothermal Steam Act of 1970
modified: Geothermal Steam Act of 1970 — adds waiver for Federal drilling permit requirement for certain geothermal activities
removed: Requirement for a Federal drilling permit for qualifying geothermal activities on non-Federal surface estate

bills.title: HEATS Act
Military Construction, Veterans Affairs, and Related Agencies Appropriations Act, FY2027
bills.likelihoodReason: Military construction and VA appropriations bills are among the least controversial annual spending bills and typically pass with bipartisan support. The House Appropriations Committee reported it, placing it on the Union Calendar. A continuing resolution fight or broader budget standoff remains the primary risk to passage this fiscal year.

items.main: Funds construction and renovation of military bases, barracks, and training facilities across all service branches.
items.detail: Covers family housing, medical facilities, and critical infrastructure upgrades at installations worldwide. Includes funding for installations in the Indo-Pacific region as part of the ongoing strategic rebalance toward countering China.

comments.text: R-Leadership: Essential for military readiness and force projection.
D-Armed Services: Supports the funding levels but wants more focus on domestic base communities.

items.main: Allocates funds for PFAS contamination cleanup at military installations.
items.detail: Addresses firefighting foam (AFFF) contamination that has polluted groundwater near dozens of bases. The cleanup mandate has bipartisan backing but the funding level is disputed — environmental groups argue it is insufficient.

comments.text: D-Environment: The allocation falls well short of EPA estimates for full remediation.
Veterans advocates: Cleanup directly tied to service-member health claims.

items.main: Funds VA hospitals, clinics, and mental health programs serving over 9 million enrolled veterans.
items.detail: Covers staffing, medical equipment, telehealth expansion, and the MISSION Act community care program which allows veterans to seek care outside the VA system. Community care has grown rapidly and now consumes a significant share of the VHA budget.

comments.text: R-VA Committee: Supports expansion of community care as a market-based solution.
D-VA Committee: Concerned that community care funding draws resources from VA facility investment.

items.main: Maintains funding for the PACT Act toxic exposure claims backlog processing.
items.detail: The PACT Act (2022) expanded eligibility for veterans exposed to burn pits, Agent Orange, and radiation. The VA faces a claims backlog running into the hundreds of thousands. This bill continues emergency processing staffing, though veterans groups say the pace remains too slow.

comments.text: Veterans of Foreign Wars: Processing times have improved but remain unacceptable for dying veterans.

items.main: Funds disability compensation, pension, education (GI Bill), and vocational rehabilitation benefits.
items.detail: The largest single line item in the bill. Disability compensation alone accounts for the majority of VBA spending. Post-PACT Act, benefit outlays have increased significantly and the appropriation reflects continued growth in the eligible veteran population.

comments.text: R-Budget: Growth in mandatory-like spending within discretionary appropriations is structurally difficult.

underreported.summary: Expands third-party administrator authority to deny VA community care referrals, effectively giving private contractors power to gatekeep which veterans can seek outside care.
underreported.why_unreported: Buried in administrative contract language; framed as 'cost management' but functionally restricts a benefit veterans assumed was guaranteed by the MISSION Act.

underreported.section: Section 412 — Relocation of Arlington Annex Operations
underreported.summary: Quietly relocates several American Battle Monuments Commission administrative functions, reducing the civilian workforce at a historic site with no public debate.
underreported.why_unreported: Grouped under 'related agencies' which receive almost no media coverage in appropriations reporting.

criticisms.why: Mental health staffing ratios at VA facilities are inadequate; the bill does not meet the 1:1500 psychiatrist-to-veteran ratio recommended by the VA's own inspector general.
Total VA discretionary spending has grown 75% since 2019; some members argue structural reform is needed before further increases.

gaps: No provision addressing the ~300,000 veteran homelessness cases despite VA housing programs being funded separately through HUD.
Silent on VA electronic health record modernization project, which has been repeatedly delayed and over-budget.
No accountability mechanism for community care contractors who deny referrals.

featured_quotes.name: Sen. Tammy Duckworth
featured_quotes.text: The mental health clinic funding is the largest single VA expansion since the PACT Act.

featured_quotes.name: Rep. Chip Roy
featured_quotes.text: We are still spending more on consultants than on actual concrete. I will vote no.

bills.brief: Must-pass appropriations bill with broad bipartisan support — the primary risk is a wider budget standoff, not the bill itself.

Adds $890M for veteran mental health clinics in 12 underserved counties
Section 223 quietly strips the standing GAO audit trigger on $1.2B in unobligated DoD funds

bills.title: Farm, Food, and National Security Act of 2026
bills.likelihoodReason: Farm bills historically pass but this one is unusually contentious. The Agriculture Committee voted 34-17 to report it — a wider party-line margin than typical farm bills. Democratic opposition to SNAP modifications and conservative pressure to cut more deeply both make floor passage and Senate negotiation difficult. A short-term extension remains likely if the bill stalls.

items.main: Updates reference prices for corn, wheat, soybeans, cotton, and other covered commodities triggering government support payments.
items.detail: The Agriculture Risk Coverage (ARC) and Price Loss Coverage (PLC) programs pay farmers when market prices fall below statutory reference levels. This bill raises those reference prices for the first time since 2014, effectively guaranteeing higher government payments regardless of market conditions.

comments.text: R-Agriculture: Reference prices haven't kept up with input cost inflation; farmers need certainty.
D-Agriculture: Raises support for large commodity operations while rural communities see no benefit.

items.main: Modifies Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program work requirements, expanding mandatory employment and training participation.
items.detail: Raises the age threshold for able-bodied adults without dependents subject to work requirements from 49 to 54. Also limits state waiver authority that previously exempted high-unemployment areas. Congressional Budget Office estimates this reduces SNAP enrollment by approximately 2-3 million participants over 10 years.

comments.text: R-Leadership: Encourages workforce participation and targets benefits to those who cannot work.
D-Nutrition: Cuts food assistance to elderly and rural Americans who face genuine barriers to employment.

items.main: Restricts purchase of U.S. agricultural land by entities linked to China, Russia, Iran, and North Korea.
items.detail: Requires divestiture of existing holdings above a threshold acreage within five years. Creates a new USDA registry of foreign-owned farmland with mandatory annual reporting. Critics note that enforcement mechanisms are vague and penalties are modest.

comments.text: R-National Security: Foreign adversary ownership near military installations is a direct security threat.
D-Agriculture: Support the concept but the enforcement structure lacks teeth.

items.main: Reauthorizes Conservation Reserve Program (CRP) with a slightly increased acreage cap, and modifies Environmental Quality Incentives Program (EQIP) payment limits.
items.detail: CRP pays farmers to take environmentally sensitive land out of production. The new cap allows enrollment of up to 27 million acres, up from 25 million. However, climate-focused conservation funding enacted in the Inflation Reduction Act is redirected into baseline programs, effectively reducing climate-specific spending.

comments.text: D-Environment: Hollows out the IRA's climate conservation investments without saying so explicitly.
R-Agriculture: Returns conservation funding to farmers rather than climate ideology.

underreported.summary: Quietly redirects approximately $18 billion in Inflation Reduction Act climate conservation funding into general EQIP and RCPP accounts, stripping the climate-specific use requirements without explicitly repealing the IRA provision.
underreported.why_unreported: Reported as a 'consolidation' of conservation programs; the IRA climate funding redirection has received almost no coverage outside of agricultural trade press despite being one of the largest effective climate policy reversals in the bill.

underreported.summary: Narrows the definition of 'bioengineered food' subject to USDA disclosure requirements, exempting highly refined products where engineered DNA is no longer detectable — effectively gutting GMO labeling for most processed foods.
underreported.why_unreported: Framed as 'technical alignment' with existing USDA standards; the practical effect is that most grocery store products that currently carry bioengineered disclosures would no longer be required to.

underreported.summary: Changes eligibility criteria for USDA rural development hospital grants in a way that excludes recently reclassified rural communities that gained suburban designation in the 2020 census.
underreported.why_unreported: Buried in the rural development title; affects dozens of small hospital systems that gained population but remain economically rural in character.

criticisms.why: SNAP modifications effectively cut food assistance to 2-3 million low-income Americans, targeting a program that is 80% of the farm bill's total cost but benefits the most vulnerable.
IRA conservation climate funding is redirected without debate, representing one of the largest rollbacks of climate investment since the IRA's passage.
Commodity reference price increases lock in higher subsidy payments regardless of market conditions, removing market discipline from agriculture policy.

gaps: No provision addressing consolidation in the meatpacking industry, where four companies control over 80% of beef processing.
Silent on crop insurance subsidies for mega-farms — the top 10% of recipients receive over 50% of payments but payment limits are unchanged.
No mechanism to address the mental health crisis in farm communities despite record farm debt and suicide rates.

featured_quotes.name: Sen. Cory Booker
featured_quotes.text: We are using a farm bill to override state environmental law. That is not what this committee was built for.

featured_quotes.name: Rep. Glenn Thompson
featured_quotes.text: American farmers cannot operate under fifty different rulebooks. This is a unity bill.

bills.brief: Contentious SNAP modifications and IRA funding redirection make Senate passage uncertain despite the inevitable farm bill tradition.
